analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to speed up and publicly report their prior-authorization decisions for seniors.
analysis.headline: A House committee voted 42-0 to send the bill to the full House; it has 304 cosponsors, including 169 Democrats and 135 Republicans, but the House has not yet voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Nearly half of Medicare beneficiaries are in private Medicare Advantage plans, which can require a doctor to get advance approval — prior authorization — before a test, surgery, or treatment. Delays and denials in that process can leave seniors waiting for care. This bill requires those plans to use a standard electronic system for approval requests, publish each year how many requests they approve or deny and how long decisions take, share their coverage rules with doctors and enrollees, and let proven providers skip the process. It does not ban prior authorization; it makes it faster and visible.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors in Medicare Advantage plans who face delays or denials when seeking care, and the doctors and hospitals that currently chase approvals by fax and phone. Patients get faster, more standardized decisions and can see each plan's approval and denial rates published online. Providers gain less paperwork and can qualify for waivers from prior-authorization requirements based on their track record.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors in Medicare Advantage plans and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans must run prior-authorization requests and supporting documents through a secure electronic system, starting in plan year 2028; faxes, plain electronic forms, and portals that do not meet federal standards would no longer count.

Plans must submit annual data that the government publishes on a public website: every service subject to prior authorization, the percentage and number of requests approved and denied, how many denials were appealed and how many appeals succeeded, the average and median hours a decision takes, and how often decisions used artificial intelligence or machine-learning tools.
Plans must give providers their coverage criteria and required documentation, and must give enrollees access to those criteria on request.

Plans must allow waivers or lighter requirements for providers who consistently follow the rules, and must review every year which services should still require prior authorization, with input from enrollees and providers.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services may set faster response deadlines for decisions, such as 24 hours, and CMS must report on real-time approvals for routinely approved services and on how AI-driven decisions affect access for rural and low-income beneficiaries.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who would have to build electronic prior-authorization systems, collect and publish detailed data on their denials and decision times, and meet standards the administration will write later. Those compliance costs could be passed on to beneficiaries through premiums or reduced plan extras. Doctors also face a transition cost in switching from fax-based processes to the new electronic system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and, possibly, premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban prior authorization or directly limit denials; it relies on transparency, electronic standards, and rules that the Secretary of Health and Human Services must still write through the regulatory process.
It excludes Part D prescription drugs, so the requirements do not reach drug coverage decisions.

The electronic-system and enrollee-protection requirements do not start until 2028, and enforcement depends on standards the administration has yet to set, leaving several years of the current process in place.
Insurers bear the cost of building the electronic systems and reporting the data, which they could pass to beneficiaries through premiums or reduced extra benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits are real but incremental: faster, standardized approvals and public visibility into each plan's denial record, rather than an end to prior authorization. The main honest objection is that the bill is largely a transparency and paperwork fix — it does not stop plans from denying care — and its strongest protections start in 2028. Against that, the costs are mostly compliance costs for insurers, and the annual public reporting on denials, appeals, and AI use gives regulators and patients the evidence base to push further later.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee unanimously voted to send the bill to the full House, but the House has not voted on it yet, and the Senate has not taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) introduced the bill on May 20, 2025, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
304 members of the House cosponsored it: 169 of the 217 House Democrats and 135 of the 223 House Republicans.
A House subcommittee considered and marked up the bill on June 25, 2026, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.
On July 15, 2026, the Ways and Means Committee voted 42-0 to order the bill reported to the full House.
The bill has not received a vote in the House or Senate, and Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has fully won or lost yet: the bill cleared committee unanimously but has not become law. The current status quo continues, under which Medicare Advantage plans set their own prior-authorization rules without the new electronic, transparency, and waiver requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare Advantage insurers, still without new rules

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Medicare; chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on July 15, 2026 and ordered the bill reported to the full House by a 42-0 vote; a subcommittee had forwarded it by voice vote on June 25, 2026.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Private insurers covering roughly half of Medicare beneficiaries
against.what_they_did: The industry has publicly urged scaling back prior-authorization legislation of this kind, warning of administrative burden and cost; no member voted against the bill in committee.

sides.party_line_note: 169 of 217 House Democrats and 135 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, and the Ways and Means Committee reported it 42-0.

industries.note: The bill makes these insurers build electronic approval systems, publish their approval and denial rates and decision times, share coverage criteria, and grant waivers to proven providers — real compliance costs and public exposure of their denial records. Prior authorization itself remains legal, so their core role and revenue stay intact; the industry's longstanding preference for keeping authorization rules flexible runs against patients' interest in timely care.

Providers replace fax-based approval processes with a standardized electronic system, get access to each plan's coverage criteria, and can qualify for waivers from prior authorization based on their track record — freeing clinician time and speeding patient care.
The mandate for standardized electronic prior-authorization transmission creates a market for the systems that meet the federal standards.

analysis.trajectory: With 304 cosponsors and a unanimous 42-0 committee vote, the bill is well positioned to reach the House floor. Versions of this same bill drew similar overwhelming House support in the previous two Congresses but never became law, so the open questions are whether leadership schedules a House vote and whether the Senate, which has not acted, takes it up — and how any final version compares to this one.
